title: Design a Library System
brief: A university library lets members search the catalogue, check books out and return them, and get reminders about due dates. Searching dominates, but a checkout must never hand the same copy to two people. At the start of each semester traffic multiplies, and a reminder job emails members through an outside provider.
constraints: Search and checkout must respond within 200 ms
About 3,000 requests per second at peak, and about 1 in 8 is a checkout or return
The same copy of a book must never be checked out to two people
The semester rush is about three times the normal load
Overdue reminders go out through an external email provider
The catalogue holds about 2 million books and 8 million loan records, for about 60,000 members

capabilities.label: Search the catalogue
capabilities.hint: Find books by title, author or subject

capabilities.label: Check out or return a book
capabilities.hint: Mark a copy as lent or returned. Two people asking for the last copy at the same moment must not both get it.

capabilities.label: Send overdue reminders
capabilities.hint: Email members whose books are overdue, about 150 per second during the sweep

queries.label: Look up the book by its ISBN
List the member's open loans, soonest due first

scenarios.title: Regular term
scenarios.interviewQuestion: Searching and checking out have very different needs. How does that change where each one runs and what it talks to?
scenarios.debrief: Search hits the index, not the database, which is kept for the few checkouts and returns.

scenarios.title: Semester rush (3x)
scenarios.description: The first week of term triples traffic.
scenarios.interviewQuestion: Locks protect checkouts but slow writes. How do you keep searching fast while checkouts queue behind locks?
scenarios.debrief: Autoscaling covers the extra volume. The cache and index take the search load, so the locked database never sees it.

scenarios.title: Primary database fails
scenarios.description: The main catalogue database loses a node.
scenarios.interviewQuestion: Which requests can still be served from a replica or a search index, and which must stop to stay correct?
scenarios.debrief: A read replica keeps reads alive, and searches never needed the primary at all.

requirements.text: Requests meet the latency target at peak
At least 98% of requests are served during the semester rush
Searching uses a search index, not the main database
Something handles checkouts, and never lends one copy twice
The design explains how the search index stays in step with checkouts
Every query is answered through a key or an index, never by reading a whole table

rubric: Search is served from a search index, with the database reserved for checkouts and returns.
Checkouts are protected by a lock or a transaction so one copy cannot be lent twice, and the throughput cost is understood.
The search index is allowed to lag slightly behind checkouts, and the design says how it catches up.
Reminders run in the background apart from request servers, behind a provider call with a timeout.
A replica or index lets search keep working if the primary database has a problem.

reference.summary: Search through an index, protect checkouts with row locks, and keep reminders in a background worker.
design: User, then a Load Balancer, then a Server (6 replicas, autoscale to 18) running both 'Search the catalogue' and 'Check out or return a book'.
Searches go through a Cache (80% hit) to a Search Index (2 replicas). Checkouts go to a Database with a read replica and Row locks.
A Worker sends overdue reminders through a Third-party API set to Email / SMS.
tradeoffs: One server for both is cheapest at this size, but a heavy search burst and a checkout share capacity.
Row locks protect the last copy of a book at the price of slower writes on a small share of traffic.
